For Richard. Written 8-Nov-26. Key dates: Capital Markets Day 25-Nov-26; Spanish general election 29-Nov-26; FY26 results in late February 2027. Sources, bases of preparation and model notes are in the end notes.

#0 Summary: key insights, implications and conclusions

Indra's earnings will keep compounding, but the share price already pays for a re-rating that Indra has not yet earned through cash conversion or index classification. The risk/reward becomes attractive at EUR 44 to 48, not at today's EUR 60.

Indra is two businesses under one ticker, and the two businesses face opposite forces. The aerospace and defence group (Defence, Air Traffic Management and Space) earns about 46% of revenue, over 70% of EBIT and holds 80% of the EUR 22.2bn backlog. It rides a Spanish rearmament cycle that is legislated, contracted and pre-financed by the state, and Indra is the state's designated integrator. The IT-services arm, Minsait, earns about 54% of revenue but under 30% of EBIT, and AI is deflating its legacy book.

The investment case is a conversion case. Indra must turn a backlog worth 3.4 times annual revenue into revenue, margin and, above all, cash. It must do so through plants that are not yet at scale, under a chief executive who has been in post for five months, and with the Spanish state acting at once as customer, financier, regulator and 28% shareholder.

The seven things that matter most

1
Indra's earnings engine is real and contracted, and consensus under-estimates FY26 earnings. The model has EBIT compounding at 14% a year, from EUR 715m in FY26 to EUR 1,207m in FY30, almost entirely through mix and absorption. Defence grows from about a third of group revenue to 45%, and the Defence margin excluding the land-vehicle business runs at about 20%. Reported FY26 EPS should be about EUR 3.00 against consensus of EUR 2.80, and the model's EUR 3.03 (before minorities) sits 8% above consensus. The FY26 results in February 2027 should therefore show an EPS beat.
2
After FY26, Viewforth's EPS sits below consensus, the gap is concentrated in three lines, and the market has not priced the gap. Viewforth's attributable EPS (after minorities) of EUR 3.23 for FY27, EUR 3.71 for FY28 and EUR 4.20 for FY29 sits 4%, 7% and 11% below consensus. Three quiet lines explain nearly all of the gap:
  • Minority interests. Other shareholders own 49% of TESS Defence and 54% of Hisdesat, so the better Indra's growth businesses perform, the more profit leaks to minorities.
  • The Minsait perimeter. Indra has sold EUR 300m of annual Minsait revenue that consensus has not yet fully removed.
  • A thin FY29 consensus. Only two brokers forecast FY29.
None of the three lines is an operating failure, and all three will reach the market through estimate cuts during 2027.
3
Cash is the weak link in the case, and the weakness comes from the structure of the financing, not from management. Reported free cash flow of about EUR 2.0bn in FY26 is customer money: it includes EUR 2.1bn of pre-financing for the Special Modernisation Programmes (PEM), which is legally a zero-interest Treasury loan that Indra repays by offsetting it against the Ministry of Defence's milestone payments. Without the pre-financing, underlying free cash flow was EUR 70m for the first nine months of 2026, and reported net cash of EUR 1.19bn becomes adjusted net debt of EUR 431m. From FY27 the pre-financing loop reverses: the model has reported free cash flow of EUR 355m to 490m a year, about 0.6 times net income, against consensus of 0.9 times. To meet the FY26 floor for comparable free cash flow (above EUR 375m), Indra needs more than EUR 305m in the fourth quarter alone.
4
The order cycle, which has historically driven defence share prices, has turned while the earnings cycle still has two years to run. Defence order intake fell 33% in 3Q26 (a book-to-bill of 0.39x) while Defence revenue rose 95%. In the defence sector, share prices have historically peaked when order growth peaked, two to three years before earnings peaked. Indra's revenue and EBIT keep compounding to 2028, but the rate of change of Defence orders turned negative in the third quarter; the EUR 1.9bn IRIS2 satellite award masked the turn at group level.
5
The share price has already paid for Indra's re-rating from IT services to sovereign defence. At 16.3x two-year-forward earnings, the stock trades at the 97th percentile of its ten-year history, whose median is 10.0x. The re-rating happened in 2024-25, and the multiple has been flat for 18 months (two-year median 15.35x). At the guideline fair multiple of 12.25x, the model's total return is -7.3% to December 2027 and +5.5% to June 2029: earnings growth adds 22% and 38% respectively, and the fall in the multiple takes away 25%.
6
One unscheduled event could change how the market values Indra: reclassification into the aerospace and defence index category. Aerospace and defence will exceed half of group revenue in FY27, at 55% on Viewforth's forecasts and 52% on consensus. That brings the revenue test of the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) within reach without a sale of Minsait; Indra already meets the STOXX 25% test. Reclassification would bring passive and benchmark buying of about 3% of free float and comparison with a defence peer group that trades at about 22x. Reclassification is the only lever that could turn the multiple from a drag into a support for the return. It is plausible within 12 to 24 months, but nobody has set a timetable for it.
7
The next four months decide whether the stock stays in its Broadening phase. The Capital Markets Day (25-Nov), the general election (29-Nov), fourth-quarter cash and the first FY27 guidance (late February) are four two-sided events within 90 days. The new chief executive describes his method as "realistic in assumptions", so he will probably set FY27 guidance floors below consensus, and a year in which Indra meets its guidance may still read as a downgrade. After February, the investment case becomes a quarterly test of the Defence margin excluding TESS and of the balance of customer advances.

Implication for Richard

Operating caseIntact and well understood
Earnings caseBetter than consensus for FY26, slightly worse beyond
Cash caseWorse than consensus on every horizon
MultipleNo cushion
Implication for Richard: the setup you look for is not present at EUR 60. You look for situations where fundamental outcomes and the probability of upgrades are unusually skewed to the positive. At EUR 60 the earnings case is sound but the cash case and the multiple leave no room for error. The setup would appear at any of three points: a price of EUR 44 to 48 (12x to 13x), a conservative FY27 guidance reset in February 2027, or a credible signal of reclassification. Indra fits your 'Demand-driven EPSU' setup in kind but arrives late in that setup: the step-up in demand is already in the share price, estimate revisions are decelerating, and the next 12 months are about proving cash conversion rather than discovering growth.

#1 Operating environment: tailwinds and headwinds

Indra's defence tailwind is legislated, contracted and pre-financed by the state, which gives Defence two to three years of revenue that is limited by capacity, not by demand. The headwinds sit in the lower-margin half of the group.

Evidence: the tailwinds are large, and the conversion of Indra's awarded programmes into revenue has barely started. Indra booked PEM revenue of EUR 97m in FY25 and expects about EUR 600m in FY26, against EUR 13.8bn awarded to it as prime contractor. Air traffic modernisation is a clean secondary tailwind, because the FAA awards are contracted and the pipeline is large.

Evidence: the headwinds are real but confined. The sell-side's rule of thumb for AI deflation in IT outsourcing is that two engineers now do the work of ten. The risk-off market regime matters because the scoring framework's own readings penalise complex and crowded investment cases in such a regime.

Inference: the defence tailwind is unusual in three respects that matter for forecasting. The spending is legislated rather than forecast, contracted rather than promised, and pre-financed rather than merely budgeted. Those three features give Defence two to three years of revenue visibility in which output is limited by Indra's capacity, not by demand. The headwinds sit in the lower-margin half of the group: Minsait and Hispasat's commercial book together earn perhaps a quarter of EBIT, and their weight shrinks each year as the mix shifts to Defence. The risk-off market regime acts on Indra's multiple, not on its earnings.

So what: forecast Defence as a capacity question. The Defence forecast should rest on plants, hiring and milestone certification. The Minsait forecast should carry a downward bias in revenue and a stable margin. The external risks are mainly matters of timing (procurement law, milestones) and of politics for the wave of programmes after 2028.

Counter-case: the tailwind rests on the least committed defence spender in NATO. Spain declined NATO's 3.5% core spending target in June 2025, has funded its uplift by decree while rolling over its 2023 budget, and holds a general election on 29-Nov-26. European competitors excluded from Spanish programmes complain that state-financed programmes "expel them from Spain". Santa Bárbara Sistemas, a General Dynamics subsidiary, has a Supreme Court challenge pending against the pre-financing decree; the court refused an injunction in April 2026, and substantive rulings are years away. A Ukraine ceasefire would also hit European defence sentiment, whatever Indra's backlog.

Where I differ from the market. The market, and both research houses whose reports are in my files, regard Spanish politics as the main external risk. I think Spanish politics is the smaller external risk for the next 18 months: both main political blocs support higher defence spending (the Partido Popular proposes more than 3% of GDP by 2030), and the EUR 13.8bn already contracted is hard to reverse. The larger external risk is one that nobody models: the legal and accounting character of the pre-financing. From 2027, that character turns the strongest tailwind (the state pays upfront) into the weakest cash line (the state is repaid by offset).

What would change my view. A post-election budget that defers the 2026-27 programme decrees (an envelope of EUR 14bn to 16bn), or a court ruling that freezes the pre-financing, would change the political and legal risk from a question of timing into a question of the level of spending.

Conclusion: Indra's external forces are among the strongest and best-contracted of any European mid-cap, and they lift earnings for two to three years; but a single state grants them, and they do not protect the multiple.
Score: 80, set by the Rater. Legislated, contracted and state-pre-financed Spanish rearmament (Indra prime on about EUR 13.8bn of PEM, conversion barely started), ReArm and European-content rules plus FAA air-traffic wins give two to three years of capacity-limited visibility on the businesses earning over 70% of EBIT, though only about 46% of revenue; AI deflation in Minsait's legacy book (-13%) and Starlink pricing at Hispasat trim it, and the political and legal threats to the spending are mostly timing (their risk is scored in topic 9); consensus sales growth at the 91st percentile is honest. Coherent with the External group's 82, just below Arteche 85 because the forces reach under half of sales rather than the core of all of it, and above RELX 76 because they are written into law and contracts.

#2 Internally driven corporate change

Corporate change at Indra is broad, well funded and pointed in the right direction, but the state decided it, the new team is stretched and unproven, and the change widens the range of outcomes before it lifts the earnings base.

Evidence: leadership. Almost the entire top of the company changed within 18 months. The executive chairman, Ángel Escribano, was conflicted: Indra was being pushed to buy his family's firm, Escribano Mechanical & Engineering (EM&E), at an escalating valuation of EUR 2.0bn to 2.5bn. SEPI, the state holding company that owns 28% of Indra, objected, Escribano was removed, and the shares fell nearly 30% in March 2026. The timeline above shows the changes that followed.

Evidence: strategy, perimeter and governance.

  • Strategy. Indra moved from an IT group with a defence arm to a sovereign aerospace, defence and space platform with an IT arm. It now has five divisions with full profit-and-loss accountability. Industrial floor space quadruples to 140,000-154,000 m2 by 2027-28, capital spending rises from about 1% to about 4% of revenue, and Indra has hired 3,000 defence staff (Defence headcount +31% to 8,424 while group headcount fell 4%).
  • Perimeter. Indra consolidated Hispasat (EUR 725m), Hisdesat and 51% of TESS Defence, the land-vehicle joint venture. It sold its business-process outsourcing unit (EUR 97m) and Minsait Business Consulting (EUR 130m enterprise value, EUR 160m of revenue), removing about 6,700 low-margin staff.
  • Governance. The chief executive's pay is 23% below his predecessor's and carries malus and clawback; board committees were merged; an independent ad hoc committee stopped the EM&E deal.
  • The new plan. The Capital Markets Day on 25-Nov-26 replaces 'Leading the Future' with 'Scale Up' 2027-30. The October 2026 investor presentation already shows the plan's main targets (below).

Inference: the direction is right and the money is there; the organisational capacity and the leadership are thin. Nine corporate-change signals fired within a year. The funding exists: net cash, a 13-year EUR 385m facility from the European Investment Bank, and EUR 800m of zero-interest loans for capacity. What Indra lacks is organisational capacity and proven leadership. It is running five plant ramps, three integrations and a reorganisation at once, under a chief executive whose record is in automotive and whose first two quarters have "reiterated" guidance rather than "raised" it.

So what: the changes raise Indra's earnings ceiling but also widen the range of outcomes, and a reset of legacy items is plausible. The ceiling rises through mix, the pruning of Minsait and the factory discipline of an automotive operator. The range widens because the classic conditions for a reset of legacy items are present: a new chairman, a new chief executive, a new auditor and a new plan, all within eight months. The candidates are capitalised development spending linked to the Future Combat Air System (FCAS) (capitalisation rose to 61% of development spending in 2025; intangibles of EUR 467m against EUR 237m), legacy TESS contracts and Minsait restructuring. Charges of EUR 50m to 150m, booked in reported rather than adjusted results at the FY26 or FY27 results, are plausible.

Counter-case: the state shareholder, not the board, decided the change, and the state could change the leadership again. SEPI has changed Indra's leadership twice in two years. The Partido Popular, likely to lead the next government, has publicly condemned SEPI's 2026 interventions, so a third leadership change within 24 months is a live risk after the election. The changes also mostly enable Indra to capture the external opportunity; they are not self-help that lifts earnings on its own.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side treats the Capital Markets Day as a catalyst for upgrades, through a margin target toward 12% and divisional bridges. I think a conservative plan is the central case, with a 65% probability. A new chief executive presenting four days before an election has every incentive to set floors he can beat, and the formal 'Scale Up' margin goal of about 10% already sits below consensus. The Capital Markets Day is more likely to improve the quality of Indra's guidance than to raise its level.

What would change my view. A Capital Markets Day that provides divisional EBIT and cash bridges, a margin schedule for TESS and a costed efficiency programme would turn the change story from narrative into measurable commitments, and would raise my confidence in FY28-29.

Conclusion: corporate change at Indra is broad, well funded and pointed in the right direction, but the state decided it, the organisation is short of people to execute it, and the new team has not yet proven it, so the change widens the range of outcomes before it lifts the earnings base.
Score: 68, set by the Rater. A large, funded pivot from IT group to sovereign aerospace-defence platform (Hispasat, Hisdesat and TESS consolidated, BPO and Business Consulting sold, floor space quadrupled, capex to about 4%, 3,000 defence hires, governance tightened) that will shift mix and earnings within three years, but it was decided by the state shareholder, mostly enables the external opportunity rather than lifting earnings by self-help, and runs under a chief executive five months in post with no defence record, five plant ramps and three integrations at once, with EUR 50m to 150m of reset charges plausible. Matches the Internal group's 68: just below Kitron 70 (real change but largely demand-driven) and above Redcare 65, whose pivot is earlier in reaching group earnings.

#3 Industry structure, business model, financial profile, management

Indra's profit engine sits in a supportive, policy-protected industry with real moats, but the state grants the home moat, Indra has no pricing or scale advantage, and its cash profile is weaker than its earnings profile.

Industry structure: concentrated and rational where Indra makes its profit, fragmented and deflating in IT services.

  • Spanish defence. A handful of prime contractors compete, and the state is consolidating share toward Indra: Indra's share of Spanish defence rose from 7% to 17%, 77% of Spanish procurement is domestic, and Article 346 of the EU treaty allows direct awards that bypass peacetime tendering.
  • European defence electronics. An oligopoly (Thales, Leonardo, Hensoldt, Saab, Indra, Rheinmetall) that is capacity-constrained and lifting margins. Competitors put margin first and often cooperate: Indra has a collaboration agreement with Thales, a memorandum of understanding with Rheinmetall, and Hanwha and IDV as platform partners.
  • Air Traffic Management. A Thales-Indra duopoly with ten-to-fifteen-year contracts, in which customers switch supplier roughly once a decade.
  • IT services. The opposite: fragmented and deflating, with Microsoft's forward-deployed engineers and challengers offering 40% to 45% discounts on legacy outsourcing. Minsait lost a EUR 20m-a-year Vodafone contract on price.

Weighted by profit, the industry structure supports Indra. It has one identifiable fragility: policy grants Indra its Spanish market share, so the share is secure while the policy lasts and reversible by politics or by law.

Business model and moat: Indra's moats are regulatory and customer-based, not cost, scale or price moats. The regulatory moats are sovereign trust, security clearances over military source code, prime-contractor status and exportability free of US International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) restrictions. The customer-based moats are installed air traffic systems and command-and-control systems embedded in national platforms for decades. Indra lacks a cost or scale moat: its capital spending was 1.6% of revenue against 5.8% at Saab and 4% at Thales, and it is subscale against Thales in radar. Its annuity income is also thin: support and sustainment is an estimated 15% to 20% of Defence revenue against 35% to 45% at peers, because the Spanish Ministry of Defence avoids multi-year maintenance contracts.

Several mechanical forces lift Indra's output each period without heroics, and the heroic part of the plan is confined to two places. The mechanical forces are backlog conversion at about 30% a year, the shift in mix, the installed base, the state's allocation of each new programme to Indra, and customer financing of working capital. The heroic part is the factory ramp and the land-vehicle business. Land vehicles are the activity furthest from Indra's electronics core, and the one where Indra's own history (a EUR 641m operating loss in 2015 on EUR 718m of charges) and sector base rates are worst.

Financial profile: above average in earnings, below average in cash.

  • Growth. Revenue grew 12.6% a year over FY21-25 (9% to 10% organic). The EBIT margin rose from 8.0% in FY23 to 9.5% in FY25, 9.8% for 9M26, and 10.4% excluding TESS. Underlying EPS grew about 25% a year over FY22-25. Reported FY25 EPS of EUR 2.48 includes a EUR 100m TESS revaluation gain that appears untaxed; clean FY25 EPS is about EUR 1.92.
  • Returns. Return on capital employed is in the mid-teens and return on equity in the low 20s. Tangible capital is tiny because customers fund working capital (net working capital excluding advances is 38% of revenue and rising), so returns on tangible capital should not be treated as structural.
  • Balance sheet. Gross debt of EUR 1.6bn costs 3.0%. Indra caps leverage below 2.0x and aims for below 1.0x.
  • Against peers. Indra's 10% to 11% EBIT margin is the lowest of its defence peers, diluted by Minsait at 7% and TESS near zero; Minsait is weak against Capgemini. Consensus has free cash flow at 0.8x to 0.9x net income; the model's 0.6x on a reported basis puts Indra nearer Saab during its ramp than Thales.

Management: a system in transition, constrained above all by state ownership.

  • The team. The team that built the 2023-25 record (targets beaten three years running) has gone. The new chief executive brings an execution vocabulary ("deliver and deliver"), serial-production discipline from the automotive industry that is directly relevant to output of the Dragon 8x8 armoured vehicle, and a clean governance structure, but no record at Indra and no defence experience. The chief financial officer, Forteza, provides continuity; he volunteered the EUR 15m underlying free cash flow figure, which is to his credit.
  • Ownership. Because the state is customer, financier, regulator and largest shareholder, Indra's strategy serves sovereignty and jobs first: Indra committed to 1,500 jobs in Catalonia within a year, and bought Hispasat from a state-influenced seller at a low return (about EUR 40m to 45m of EBIT on EUR 725m).
  • Culture. Congruence between management and shareholders is low: four chief executives since 2022, 40.5% of votes against the pay report, executive ownership under 0.05%, and an incentive plan whose EUR 630m cash hurdle prepayments can satisfy.
  • Ambition. Very large: near-doubling revenue in four years, becoming global number one in air traffic, and building EUR 1bn businesses in both Space and sovereign AI. The predecessors and the state set that ambition, not the new team.
Where I differ from the market. Consensus and the two research houses frame Indra as an "IT conglomerate becoming defence champion" and place the quality debate in TESS's dilution of margins and in Minsait. I place the quality debate in two other places. First, the state grants Indra's home moat, which is why pricing power is a political question (see #5). Second, the share of recurring sustainment revenue is low, so Indra's installed base yields less annuity income than Thales's or Saab's, and Indra's earnings remain more dependent on new programmes than a defence multiple assumes.

What would change my view. Evidence that the Spanish Ministry of Defence is moving to multi-year sustainment contracts, or TESS reaching margins of 3% to 5% within 2027, would raise my view of the quality of Indra's business model.

Conclusion: Indra has a strongly supportive, policy-protected industry structure around a profit engine with real but state-granted moats, an above-average earnings profile and a below-average cash profile, run by a credible but unproven team that answers first to the state.
Score: 58, set by the Rater. Qualitatively a concentrated, policy-protected structure (Thales-Indra duopoly in air traffic, state consolidating Spanish defence toward Indra) with sovereign and installed-base moats, but the home moat is state-granted, there is no pricing or scale moat, sustainment is only 15-20% of Defence, Minsait (54% of revenue) sits in a fragmented, AI-deflating market, and management is new, state-led and low-congruence (group 40). ROIC 18% (88th percentile) and ROE 90th flatter a business whose tangible capital is customer-funded, while operating margin is at the 34th percentile and forward cash conversion about 0.6x; weighing the groups (65, 58, 62, 40) puts it just below Helios Towers 60 and above Shell 54.

#4 Guidance conservatism and the record of delivery

Indra will very probably meet its FY26 guidance floors, but free cash flow is the stretch item, and the first FY27 guidance will probably sit below consensus, so the guidance setup is neutral rather than favourable.

Evidence: the FY26 floors depend on a strong fourth quarter. Indra gives FY26 guidance as floors: revenue above EUR 7,000m in local currency (raised earlier in 2026 from above EUR 6,000m, mostly for perimeter changes), EBIT above EUR 700m, comparable free cash flow above EUR 375m, Defence growth of about 80% and a Defence margin of 18% to 19%. The table below shows what the fourth quarter must deliver after nine months. To reach 18% to 19% for the year, the fourth-quarter Defence margin must exceed 21%.

Evidence: the record of beats is strong, but 2026 has been weaker. Under the previous chief executive, Indra beat its revenue and EBIT guidance by 4% to 10% for three years (FY25: revenue +4.9%, EBIT +5.5%, free cash flow +21%). In 2026, Indra reiterated its EBIT floor twice after a first half that ran ahead. Third-quarter revenue missed consensus by 3% and Defence revenue missed by 17%. After the third quarter, Bernstein trimmed its FY26 operating estimates (revenue EUR 6,970m, EBIT EUR 698m) while raising EPS through below-the-line items.

Inference: conservatism survives at group level, but the FY26 beat now rests on one quarter and mostly on items below the operating line. The floors will very probably be met (85%), and EPS will be beaten, mainly through a 16.7% third-quarter tax rate and through a EUR 36m dividend from ITP and a EUR 17m reclassification gain in the financial result. The beat machine of 2023-25 has not stopped, but it has become lumpier, and, as a year ago, it now rests on the fourth quarter. The free cash flow floor is the only line that could miss by a margin the market would punish; I put the probability of meeting it at 55% to 60%.

So what: anchor FY26 just above the floors, and expect the first FY27 guidance to sit below consensus. The model has FY26 revenue of EUR 7,023m, EBIT of EUR 715m and reported EPS of about EUR 3.00. For the first FY27 guidance in late February 2027, my central case is shown in the table below. The probability that the market receives that guidance as conservative rather than as a cut is about 50%, depending on how much the Capital Markets Day has already reset expectations.

Counter-case: the floors may be sandbagged again. Management has said informally that it has "high confidence" in FY26, and it raised the Defence growth outlook to 80% in a weak quarter. Morgan Stanley's FY26 EBIT forecast (EUR 804m) sits 13% above consensus. If the fourth quarter repeats the pattern of 4Q25, Indra beats EBIT guidance by 3% to 5%. The new chief executive's incentive to set targets he can beat is the same as his predecessor's.

Where I differ from the market. Consensus treats Indra's guidance as conservative and treats the record as a reason to forecast above it. I forecast above guidance only for FY26 EPS, and only slightly for FY26 EBIT. For FY27, I expect the "conservative floor" to land below the sell-side's forecasts, so the next guidance event has as much chance of reading as a downgrade as of reading as a reassurance. The reason is a change of phase, not of management style. The 2023-25 beats came in an organic, engineering-led phase. 2026-28 is a phase of physical industrial expansion: the kind of phase in which Indra's own record failed (2011-15) and in which peers most often stumble. Rheinmetall reset its FY26 guidance in November after EUR 1.69bn of negative operating free cash flow, and Saab cut its cash-conversion target to 60%.

What would change my view. Fourth-quarter comparable free cash flow above EUR 350m and FY27 floors at or above consensus would restore Indra's standing as a serial beater and would lift my FY27 forecasts.

Conclusion: Indra's guidance is conservative in style and will be met in FY26, but with a thinner margin of safety than the record implies and with free cash flow as the stretch item; the first FY27 floors will probably sit below consensus, so the guidance setup is neutral rather than favourable.
Score: 62, set by the Rater. Three years of 4-10% beats on revenue and EBIT under the previous team and FY26 floors very likely met (85%), but the delivering team has gone, the EBIT floor has only been reiterated twice, 3Q26 missed on revenue (-3%) and Defence (-17%), the cash floor is a 55-60% call, consensus already sits at the floors and the first FY27 guidance is likely below consensus. Coherent with the Guidance group's 55 and Sell-side group's 45 lifted by a clean multi-year record with no cut: below MITIE 64 because current conservatism is thin, above Renew 59 which actually cut.

#5 How revenue growth becomes profit growth: pricing, leverage, cost, loops

EBIT grows about twice as fast as revenue through mix and absorption, but Indra has no pricing power, its operating leverage is asymmetric and most exposed in FY27, and the items below EBIT turn against EPS and cash from FY27.

Pricing power: close to none in real terms. Sovereignty pays Indra in win rates, contract length and backlog, not in price.

  • Spanish defence. Prices on direct awards are negotiated on cost under state audit and statutory profit limits. The Dragon 8x8 contract is long-term and fixed-price, with pre-set milestones. Escalation clauses pass materials inflation on to the state, so prices rise 1.5% to 2.5% in nominal terms and about zero in real terms.
  • Air traffic. Contracts run ten to fifteen years at stable prices, but Indra wins abroad partly on price: Thales USA protested that Indra's FAA bid was "unrealistically low".
  • Minsait and Hispasat. Minsait's legacy prices deflate by a low-to-mid single-digit percentage each year; Hispasat's commercial capacity prices deflate 2% to 3% a year.

Net, price adds about 0 to 0.5 points to revenue growth and is a 0.2 to 0.4 point annual drag on margin before mix, because personnel costs (about half of revenue) inflate 4% to 6% per head. The one place where a real price premium could appear, Spanish sovereign defence, is the place where the state, as customer, financier and shareholder, caps it.

Operating leverage: moderate, rising and asymmetric. Indra's incremental EBIT margins were 17.8% (FY23-24), 13.2% (FY24-25) and 14.7% (1H25-1H26), on an average margin near 10%. The model implies 20% in FY27 (revenue +EUR 604m, EBIT +EUR 121m, +17%) and 17.6% in FY28 (revenue +EUR 785m, EBIT +EUR 138m, +16.5%), so EBIT grows about twice as fast as revenue. What has changed is the fixed share of the cost base: depreciation rises from 2.2% of revenue in FY25 to about 4% (satellites and plants), Defence engineers are kept on through troughs, and five plants are commissioning.

The asymmetry is the key point: a euro of revenue that arrives drops through to EBIT at about 18%, but a euro of Defence revenue that fails to arrive, after the plants and engineers are in place, costs 25% to 30%. FY27 is the year of maximum exposure. The third quarter of 2026 demonstrated the asymmetry: revenue 3% below consensus produced a 9.4% EBIT margin against 9.8% for nine months, and Defence revenue 17% below expectations produced a four-point fall in the divisional margin. Bernstein's symmetric sensitivity (each point of revenue moves EPS by 1.13%) therefore understates the downside.

Financial leverage: none on EPS, and a state subsidy that fades. Indra's net cash is customer money. Interest earned on about EUR 2.6bn to 3bn of gross cash, much of it zero-interest state pre-financing, more than offsets the cost of EUR 1.6bn of gross debt at 3%. That interest income, plus the implicit benefit of the zero-interest loans recognised under IAS 20 and IFRS 9, is worth about EUR 45m to 65m a year before tax, or 6% to 8% of FY26-27 EPS: a state subsidy embedded in earnings. The subsidy shrinks as advances are consumed and will not renew when programme funding moves to Ministry of Defence budgets by 2030. Indra's sensitivity to interest rates is therefore on the asset side: its EPS rises with rates, the reverse of a normal industrial company. Indra has no buyback lever (the share count is flat at about 175m, with repurchases only for executive plans) and issues no shares.

Cost-out: a gross pool of EUR 100m to 150m a year by FY28, mostly absorbed. Consolidating tier-1 suppliers (fewer than 450 suppliers now account for 90% of spend) has saved more than 10% on key radar families and halved radar lead times. A further 3% to 5% saving on EUR 2.5bn of Defence purchases by FY29 is worth EUR 40m to 75m, arriving at serial volumes in FY28-29 and partly passed back to a customer that audits costs. Pruning Minsait adds EUR 25m to 30m. Against those savings stand wage indexation (about EUR 17m per percentage point), plant start-up costs and a national champion's political need to add jobs. The net saving that reaches EBIT is 0.3 to 0.5 points of margin over FY27-29, already inside the model's path. The model includes no separate cost programme, so a costed programme at the Capital Markets Day would be upside.

Feedback loops: reinforcing above EBIT to FY28, balancing below EBIT from FY27. The figure below lists the loops. The prepayment loop is the most important balancing loop: each euro of programme revenue brings only about 85 cents of cash, because advances are offset against milestone payments. The hinge loop is capacity absorption, which reinforces earnings if deliveries keep pace with the plants and turns sharply against them if deliveries do not; the third quarter of 2026 was the first sign of strain.

So what: EPS grows more slowly than EBIT from FY27, and free cash flow grows slowest of all. Revenue growth of 8% to 10% a year converts into EBIT growth of 14% to 17% a year to FY28, which then fades to 14% in FY29 and 9% in FY30. In FY27, attributable EPS grows 11% against EBIT growth of 17%, because the below-the-line tailwinds of FY21-26 become mild headwinds. Over FY21-26, the tax rate fell from 31% to about 25%, interest income rose, a one-off gain arrived and minorities were negligible. From FY27, the tax rate rises to 26% to 27%, the financial result is flat to worse, and minorities take 4% to 5% of profit.

Where I differ from the market. The market debates the TESS margin. For EPS, the Defence margin excluding TESS matters about four times more, because 49% of every euro TESS earns leaves through minorities. Two points of margin on the EUR 2.15bn of Defence revenue outside TESS is worth EUR 0.18 of EPS; TESS moving from a 0% to a 2% margin on EUR 0.85bn is worth EUR 0.04. The market is watching the right division and the wrong line.

What would change my view. Disclosure of a TESS margin path and of plant run-rates at the Capital Markets Day would let me turn the asymmetry into a schedule. A Spanish move to loosen cost-based pricing would add a lever I have not modelled.

Conclusion: revenue growth does produce outsized EBIT growth (about two to one) through mix and absorption, but Indra has no pricing power, its operating leverage is asymmetric and most exposed in FY27, its financial leverage is a fading subsidy rather than an amplifier, and the loops below EBIT turn against EPS and cash from FY27.
Score: 50, set by the Rater. EBIT grows about twice revenue through mix and absorption (incremental margins 13-20% on a 10% average) and the fixed share of costs is rising with plants and satellite depreciation, but there is no real pricing power (cost-based, state-audited Defence pricing, deflating Minsait and Hispasat), financial leverage is nil and its interest subsidy fades, net cost-out is only 0.3-0.5 points, and minorities, tax and the financial line make attributable EPS grow only about 1.4 times revenue, below the Universe's typical 2x. Ordinary mix with gearing that is asymmetric on the downside, consistent with groups of 62 and 60 only after their non-structural strengths are set aside.

Scope for double-digit growth: yes; scope for higher margins than in the past: yes. EBIT compounds at 14% a year over FY26-30 (18.6% from FY25), against 22% over FY23-25. The EBIT margin reaches 12.4% by FY30, against a FY19-25 range of 0.2% to 9.5%. Attributable EPS compounds at about 12% a year from FY26; FY26 itself is up about 52% on the clean FY25 base of EUR 1.92. Organic revenue growth of 9% to 11% continues the pace of FY21-25, but Defence now leads instead of Minsait. The jump in EBITDA margin from 11.7% to 14.1% is mostly satellite depreciation and perimeter changes, so EBIT is the honest line to judge margins by.

Where Viewforth's forecasts differ from consensus, and why.

  • FY26. EPS is above consensus (tax, financial income, nine months already reported); revenue and EBIT are at the guidance floors.
  • FY27. Revenue is 4% below consensus, because Minsait Business Consulting has been sold, Minsait's organic growth was 1% in 3Q26 with a 0.89x book-to-bill, and Space is shrinking organically by 17% to 20%. EBIT is 3% below. Attributable EPS is 4% below, and minorities explain the whole EPS gap, because the model's EPS before minorities of EUR 3.41 matches consensus (chart below).
  • FY28-29. Revenue is 5% to 8% below consensus, because the EUR 10bn target for 2029 needs acquisitions and the model includes only EUR 150m a year of bolt-ons. EPS is 7% to 11% below, because of minorities and a FY29 consensus that rests on two brokers.
  • Cash. Well below consensus on every horizon: capital spending runs above the guided 4.0% to 4.3% of revenue (EUR 374m in the first nine months against EUR 42m a year earlier), and advances are consumed from FY27.

Range of outcomes: narrow for FY26, wide for FY27 and FY28.

  • FY26. Narrow, because nine months are known: reported EPS EUR 2.90 to 3.05; comparable free cash flow EUR 300m to 430m.
  • FY27. Attributable EPS EUR 2.65 to 3.65 around a base of EUR 3.23, with about a quarter of the probability in each tail. The operating skew is negative (plants ahead of volume, FCAS phasing, Dragon penalties, a possible reset), and the below-the-line skew is positive (a tax rate nearer 25%, interest income, non-operating gains like those in 3Q26). Reported free cash flow EUR 150m to 500m around EUR 355m.
  • FY28. EPS EUR 3.2 to 4.3 around EUR 3.71.
Where I differ from the market. The market frames Indra as a "20% EPS compounder" (Morgan Stanley, to 2030). I frame Indra as a 14% EBIT compounder, a 12% EPS compounder and a 0.6x cash converter. The difference does not lie in demand or in the Defence margin excluding TESS, where I am close to consensus. It lies in the lines the sell-side guides least: minorities, perimeter, capital spending and advances.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Over the next 6 to 12 months, estimates and the narrative are more likely to move down than up, apart from FY26 EPS in February; that is the opposite of what the case needs at a 97th-percentile multiple.

Guidance: a met FY26 and a FY27 starting point below consensus are the most likely events. The figure below gives the probabilities. An in-year raise of FY27 guidance would most likely come for perimeter changes at the July 2027 results, as it did in 2024 and 2026. For the medium term, the Capital Markets Day will probably raise the margin target toward 12% by 2030 (already in the October presentation) and keep the political target of EUR 10bn of revenue by 2029, which needs acquisitions. It will probably also keep the cumulative cash target of EUR 2.0bn to 2.5bn. On the model's comparable path (about EUR 2.2bn), Indra meets that cash target only at the low end, and only because the definition helps: it excludes prepayments and assumes constant factoring, although Indra has eliminated factoring.

Sell-side estimates: up for FY26 EPS in February, then down for everything else through 2027. The table below sets out the expected moves. Two points explain them. First, the FY27 EPS cut comes in two steps: a perimeter cut of about 4% to revenue, partly offset as brokers follow Bernstein in lowering tax and raising financial income; Bernstein has already moved its FY27 EPS from EUR 3.13 to 3.61 on exactly that logic. Second, the FY29 consensus currently rests on two brokers, and as the cautious cluster (Bestinver, UBS, GVC Gaesco) publishes FY29 forecasts and brokers recognise minorities, FY28-29 estimates fall. The breadth of revisions, rated A today, is more likely to fade to B or C than to strengthen, and the breadth reading is the framework's most reliable marker of a case moving from reinforcing to stalling.

Narrative: the question has already moved from growth to the profitability and cash of that growth. The market's question has moved from "can Indra grow?" to "how profitable and cash-generative is Indra's growth?" (Bernstein: "Beyond the order boom, cash is the question"). The next narrative moves will turn on execution proof points: Dragon output near 100 vehicles a year, the As Pontes plant coming on stream and radar production in Kansas. They will also turn on the advances balance starting to fall and, if the Capital Markets Day supplies them, on divisional bridges that make the case monitorable. The one positive narrative step with real power is reclassification (see #8 and #10), and nobody has scheduled it.

Where I differ from the market. Two houses (Morgan Stanley at EUR 3.64 and Bernstein at EUR 3.61 for FY27 EPS) sit at my upside case; the visible low cluster of brokers (EUR 3.04 to 3.21) sits at my base. Consensus does not yet include the quiet negatives, which will arrive through estimate cuts: Bernstein models minorities at EUR 8m to 15m against EUR 12.7m already booked in nine months and EUR 28m in my FY27; capital spending runs above the guided ratio; and the Paz II satellite programme, financed by a EUR 1,011m repayable state loan, sits inside capital spending. Consensus does not include the quiet positives either (a tax rate nearer 25% than the 29% to 30% the bears assume, the FY26 reported beat, and reclassification), and two of those positives arrive sooner.

What would change my view. A Capital Markets Day that turns the EUR 10bn revenue target for 2029 into a costed path with acquisitions would hold revenue estimates even as margin estimates are trimmed. A fourth-quarter cash beat would hold cash estimates for a quarter.

Conclusion: the skew of revisions is positive for FY26 EPS in February and negative for FY27-29 EPS, revenue and cash through 2027, so over 6 to 12 months estimates and the narrative are more likely to move down than up, which is the opposite of the setup the case needs at this multiple.
Score: 30, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is likely only met for FY26 and reset below consensus for FY27 (65%), with a 12% CMD margin target already in the October presentation; consensus FY27 EPS likely cut 3-6% and FY28-29 7-11% (about -0.4 to -0.5 times revenue growth) plus 15-20% on cash, against a near-term FY26 EPS beat in February; the narrative has moved to cash and execution and is more likely to worsen. Coherent with the fourth set's 33: below TT Electronics 33 because guidance itself leans down, above Indutrade 28 because the FY26 beat and an unscheduled reclassification give some offset.

#8 Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, price, and peers

Momentum is still positive on every reading but decelerating on all of them, and upgrades are migrating from operating lines to non-operating lines.

Guidance momentum: positive but decelerating. Indra raised guidance once in 2026 (the revenue floor to above EUR 7,000m, mostly for perimeter changes), raised its Defence growth outlook to about 80% in October, and reiterated its EBIT floor twice after a first half that ran ahead. Indra has not raised its profit guidance since it set the floors.

Sell-side momentum: strong and fading, with the latest upgrades coming from margin and below-the-line items rather than revenue. The table below shows how the twelve-month rise in FY27 consensus has slowed to almost nothing in the last month. The share of Buy ratings is 61% (+3 points in a month, -2 in three months, +8 in six months), the revision-momentum score is 13, and the dashboard's Sell-side Earnings Momentum grade has been pinned at A (24-Oct-26), the best in its sector. After the third quarter, Bernstein raised its target price to EUR 73 and raised EPS while trimming operating estimates: the first visible rotation from operating to non-operating upgrades.

Peers: the IT-services basket in which Indra is listed has no bearing on its shares, and defence peers are split exactly as Indra is split internally. Against the IT-services basket, Indra's six-month correlation is 0.28, its beta 0.43, and the basket explains 8% of its share-price variance. The basket rose 27% over six months while Indra rose 13%, and most of the basket (Capgemini, Sopra Steria, Alten, Neurones) sits at the bottom of its ten-year P/E range with negative earnings momentum (Capgemini graded F, Sopra D). Among defence peers, electronics and sensors are being upgraded while platforms and cash are being cut (figure below). Saab's sell-side ratings are heavily Underweight on valuation despite its delivery. European defence trades at about 22x earnings, and Redburn notes that Indra trades well below that level.

Where I differ from the market. The dashboard's A grade for earnings momentum looks backward, and the market reads the +32% twelve-month revision as momentum. The one-month and three-month revisions (+2% and +4%) and the shift of upgrades to below-the-line items say that earnings momentum is in its last innings. I would weight the rate of change of revisions above their level.

What would change my view. A Capital Markets Day that lifts FY28-30 EBIT estimates, together with a fourth-quarter cash beat, would re-accelerate revisions into 2027.

Conclusion: momentum is still positive on every reading but decelerating on all of them: upgrades are migrating from operating to non-operating lines, price momentum is fading from the top decile, and the defence peer group is itself moving from an orders-driven to an execution-driven phase.
Score: 78, set by the Rater. Both measures positive but relative strength short of the top fifth, with no part strongly negative, gives B. I place it in the lower half of the band because every part is decelerating: revisions +32% over twelve months but +4% over three and +2% over one and migrating below the operating line, guidance held rather than raised, narrative softening after 3Q26, price below its 50-day though above a rising 200-day, and defence peers split.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the case

Indra is a simple earnings engine inside a complicated chassis: four variables drive almost everything, but the main risks are correlated through one customer, one financing mechanism and one factory ramp, and the fair trough is about 30% below today's price.

Simplicity of drivers: high. Four variables generate almost all of the difference between the forecasts and the past (figure above). Air Traffic Management, Minsait's margin and Mobility act as stabilising ballast, together about a quarter of EBIT. The direction of Indra's earnings is as predictable as any European mid-cap's, and the level of earnings to FY27 is predictable within about 5% with 60% confidence.

Complexity of the case: high. The chassis around the four drivers is unusually complicated, as the figure lists: Indra carries eleven live change items against a guardrail of two.

Fragilities and requirements: five fragilities, and the first three are correlated. Milestone certification, serial production at TESS and the legal character of the pre-financing all run through one customer, one financing mechanism and one factory ramp. Milestone certification moves revenue, margin and restricted cash at once, so the three main risks tend to strike together.

Suddenness, trackability and materiality: the sudden risks are large, and several key risks cannot be tracked from company disclosure. A Ukraine ceasefire headline would hit the whole sector by 15% to 25%. A SEPI-driven board change cost nearly 30% in days in March 2026. A fourth-quarter cash miss has Rheinmetall's 2026 experience as its precedent. Investors can track the Defence margin, book-to-bill, Minsait intake, Space growth, the advances balance, tax and minorities each quarter, but must rely on the Spanish press for Dragon acceptances and cannot see plant run-rates, the offset schedule or the court calendar.

Sector and cyclical precedents: the share price can stall on orders while earnings keep compounding.

  • Orders lead share prices. Defence equities have peaked when order growth peaked, well before revenue peaked, as in the US build-up of the 1980s. Indra's Defence intake fell 33% in 3Q26 while Defence revenue rose 95%.
  • Ramps deliver revenue on time and profit and cash late. Saab carried start-up costs on the T-7 trainer, Leonardo lost more than EUR 200m in aerostructures, Hensoldt had a near-zero quarter in Sensors during a site move, and Rheinmetall's cash disappointed in 2026.
  • Indra's own history is the strongest warning. Its operating margin went from +10% in 2011 to a EUR 641m loss in 2015 through fixed-price projects in new activities, and in 2020 Indra withdrew guidance when a 5% revenue fall took EBIT to zero.
  • IT services under AI deflation. Atos fell 56% in a year; that is the read-across for the Minsait label the ticker still carries.

Downside to a fair trough: about 30% in the central case. A fair trough multiple for a hybrid group with over 70% of EBIT in defence is nearer 11x to 12x than the 8x to 10x of Indra as an IT-services company.

  • Mild: 12.5x to 13x on intact two-year-forward EPS of about EUR 3.7 gives EUR 47 to 49 (-20%).
  • Central: 11x gives about EUR 41 (-31%), near the 52-week low of EUR 42.55.
  • Severe: 11x on EPS cut by 10% to 15% gives EUR 35 to 37 (-40%), which is also Morgan Stanley's bear case.
Where I differ from the market. The bear case is crowded into governance and cash quality (the short positions, the 40.5% vote against pay) and is empty where I think the risk sits: FY27's asymmetric operating leverage, minorities, and capital spending above the guided ratio. The bull case treats the prepayment cash as a strategic advantage, because it provides cheap funding and avoids bank debt. The prepayment cash is an advantage, but it is also the single mechanism that will make Indra's reported cash disappoint for four years.

What would change my view. Disclosure of a milestone and offset schedule, or a Minsait partnership that simplifies the perimeter, would reduce both the complexity of the case and the correlation of its risks.

Conclusion: the case is simple in its drivers and complex in its chassis; its risks are correlated through one customer, one financing mechanism and one factory ramp; the fair trough is about 30% below today's price; and sector precedents warn that the share price can stall on orders while earnings keep compounding, so Indra's riskiness is well above the European average.
Score: 40, set by the Rater. The memo's FY27 EPS cone is EUR 2.65-3.65 around 3.23 (about -18%/+13%, a quarter of the probability in each tail) with negative operating skew, and the few drivers sit in a complex chassis whose main risks are correlated through one customer, one pre-financing mechanism and one factory ramp (Dragon deliveries behind plan with penalties), with sudden events (ceasefire, SEPI board change, a cash miss, a reset charge) and a 30% downside to a fair trough at a 97th-percentile multiple; net cash keeps the balance sheet out of it. Groups at 42 and 48: below OMV Petrom 44 and above Fevertree 39, and well below NKT 54, which has a similar prepayment-funded ramp without the political, legal and perimeter complexity.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

The dashboard's rule says Broadening, and the earnings agree; but five leading indicators of Stalling have turned at once, and together they look like the quarter before a stall.

The dashboard's rule says Broadening, and the earnings evidence agrees. Indra's thesis has broadened from Defence electronics to air traffic (FAA awards, division revenue +39%), Space (EUR 1.9bn of intake from the EU's IRIS2 secure-satellite constellation) and sovereign AI (IndraMind). The backlog has risen 133% in a year, revenue and EBIT reinforce each other to FY28, and the re-rating has partly happened.

My view: late Broadening, with the leading indicators of Stalling already switched on. Five readings mark the turn:

  1. Order intake has peaked: Defence book-to-bill was 0.39x in 3Q26, and the PEM wave was front-loaded in 2025-26.
  2. Guidance has been reiterated twice rather than raised, and the next guidance event will probably reset below consensus.
  3. Revisions are decelerating, from +32% over twelve months to +2% over one month, and migrating to non-operating lines.
  4. The multiple has been flat for 18 months at 15x to 16x after rising from 8.7x, and the stock under-performed its nominal sector by 14 points over six months.
  5. Price momentum has fallen from the 92nd to the 71st percentile.

None of the five readings is yet a Stalling reading; together, they are what the quarter before a stall looks like.

Probabilities over 12 months: Stalling is the most likely phase, at 45%.

  • Stalling, 45%: estimates flat to down, the multiple drifts to 12x to 14x, the shares stay range-bound.
  • Continued Broadening, 35%: the Capital Markets Day sets credible bridges, fourth-quarter cash delivers, estimates hold, and the multiple holds at 15x to 16x.
  • Reinforcing, 20%: a reclassification is signalled or a Minsait partnership is agreed, the market adopts a defence multiple, and the multiple reaches 18x or above.
  • Collapsing, about 10% (inside the Stalling tail): execution failure plus a reversal of prepayments, with the multiple at 11x or below.
Where I differ from the market. The sell-side's rating mix (61% Buy, mean target EUR 69.58) and the dashboard's A grade for earnings momentum describe a stock in its Reinforcing or Broadening phase. The evidence from the rate of change describes a stock approaching the end of Broadening. The disagreement is about timing, not direction, and timing is what the multiple pays for.

What would change my view. Fourth-quarter comparable cash above EUR 350m, FY27 floors at or above consensus and a Capital Markets Day with divisional bridges would keep the stock in Broadening through 2027. A reclassification announcement would move it to Reinforcing.

Conclusion: the stock is in Broadening by the rule and by its earnings, but orders, guidance style, the breadth of revisions, the multiple and price momentum all point to a stall within two to four quarters, unless the next four months reset the market's frame.
Score: 48, set by the Rater. The computed Broadening is right on earnings (backlog +133%, EBIT compounding to FY28), but the leading indicators of a stall are on: Defence book-to-bill 0.39x, guidance reiterated not raised and likely reset below consensus, revisions decelerating and turning to non-operating lines, the multiple plateaued for 18 months and relative strength down from 92nd to 71st; the memo's 45% stall weighting fits. Late Broadening edging to Stalling: just below BP 50 (late Reinforcing) and above Linea Directa 45.

#11 The fair multiple

The guideline's 12.25x is the fair multiple for Indra as it is today; 14x needs proof of cash or a reclassification, and today's 16x needs both. The 22% gap to the current multiple is a real headwind, not an artefact of Indra's IT-services past.

The guideline: 12.25x two-year-forward earnings, 22% below today's 15.7x to 16.3x. For a stock in the Broadening phase, the guideline sets the fair multiple at the 80th percentile of the stock's own ten-year range. That range has a 10th percentile of 7.3x, a median of 10.0x, a 75th percentile of 11.8x and a 90th percentile of 13.6x.

My view: the guideline sits at the low end of a fair range of about 12x to 14x, and I would set the central fair multiple at about 13x. Three arguments pull in different directions:

  • The ten-year history belongs to a different company. The ten-year range belongs to an IT-services group that traded at 7x to 13x; the company now earns over 70% of EBIT in defence electronics and air traffic. A sum of the parts on FY27 EBIT gives about 14x: Defence, Air Traffic and Space (about EUR 590m) at 16x, a discount to the 20x-plus of European defence peers for state ownership and execution, and Minsait and Mobility (about EUR 235m) at 9x. That 14x is the undiscounted frame.
  • A discount is deserved today. A conglomerate, governance and cash-quality discount of 10% to 15% (Morgan Stanley applies 15%) takes 14x down to about 12x to 12.6x, where the guideline sits. Indra deserves the discount while the state decides its leadership, while its cash conversion is unproven in the ramp, and while its two halves remain stapled together.
  • Phase and risk argue for the lower half of the range. In a late Broadening phase, with decelerating revisions and correlated risks, forecasts are more uncertain, so the multiple should sit lower in the range, not higher.

Each step up in the multiple needs a proof that Indra has not yet given, and the market already pays for the highest step. 12.25x is fair for today's Indra, as currently governed, classified and converting cash. 14x is fair for an Indra that has proven its cash through one ramp year or been reclassified. 16x, today's level, needs both, or the full defence-sector frame.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side's targets (mean EUR 69.58, median EUR 70) imply about 17x to 18x FY28 EPS of EUR 4.00, which is the full defence frame applied now. I think the defence frame is available only to a company that converts at least 0.8x of earnings into cash or sits in a defence index. On my forecasts, Indra will do neither within 18 months.

What would change my view. A reclassification signal, or a Minsait partnership at a valuation above 10x EV/EBIT, would move my central fair multiple to 14x. A fourth-quarter cash miss or a post-election leadership change would move it to 11x to 12x.

Conclusion: the guideline's 12.25x is defensible as the fair multiple for the stock as it is today; it is the low end of a 12x to 14x range whose top needs proof that the company cannot deliver within 18 months, so the 22% gap to the current multiple is a real headwind, not an artefact of the stock's IT-services past.
Score: 21, set by the Rater. Dear on both gives F: against its own history it is at the top, and on the memo's peer comparison it trades far richer against its IT cohort than it normally has. Step 2: the perimeter has changed, so part of the premium is deserved (defence peers about 22x), which lifts it to the top of the band, but the memo's own fair range of 12-14x needs cash proof or reclassification it is unlikely to get within 18 months, so 16.3x is still about a quarter too dear and the letter holds.

#12 Total shareholder return

Earnings growth of 22% over 18 months is swamped by a 25% de-rating to the guideline multiple: the model's return is -7.3% to December 2027. The return turns clearly positive only if the multiple holds, or at an entry price in the mid-40s.

The model's return at the guideline multiple. The model reaches 12.25x at the 18-month column and uses two-year-forward EPS before minorities.

HorizonTotal returnAnnualisedValue per shareDividendsMultipleEarnings
18 months, to 31-Dec-27-7.3%-6.4%EUR 55.57+1.3%-25.0%+21.9%
Three years, to 30-Jun-29+5.5%+2.0%EUR 63.19+2.2%-25.0%+37.6%

What drives the return: earnings do the work and the multiple undoes it. Two-year-forward EPS rises from about EUR 3.68 today to about EUR 4.49 at December 2027 (+22%) and about EUR 5.05 at June 2029 (+38%), which is the 12% to 14% annual compounding of #6 showing through in the return. The multiple falls from 16.3x to 12.25x (-25%); over 18 months the fall is larger than the earnings gain, and over three years the earnings gain roughly cancels it. Dividends add 1.3% and 2.2%: with a payout ratio of 13% to 18% and a yield of 0.6%, cash returns are irrelevant to the case. Indra has no buybacks to add a per-share gain.

Two adjustments Richard should make.

  1. Use attributable EPS. The model's EPS is before minorities. On attributable EPS (about EUR 4.20 to 4.25 two years forward at December 2027), the 18-month value at 12.25x is about EUR 51.5, the return is about -13%, and the three-year return is about zero.
  2. Do not use the model's net cash for an enterprise-value cross-check. The model's balance sheet overstates net cash by about EUR 1.9bn through a double count of the first-half inflow. The overstatement does not affect the P/E-based return (end note 6).

The return at other multiples (18 months, model EPS of about EUR 4.49, dividends +1.3%).

Over three years, each turn of multiple matters even more. At 14x the three-year return is about +20% (6% a year), and at 16.3x it is about +40% (12% a year). At the 18-month point, each turn of multiple is worth about EUR 4.5 a share, or 7.5% of today's price.

Where the return is unusually skewed, and where it is not: the skew is negative at EUR 60 and turns positive below about EUR 48. The earnings term is well supported by the contracted backlog, nine months of FY26 already reported and the mechanical shift in mix; I would put its 18-month range at +15% to +28%. The multiple term is the whole argument: at 16x, the share price already prices the outcome (cash proof or reclassification) that could justify a fair multiple of 14x to 16x. Below about EUR 48 (13x FY28 attributable EPS), a 15% annualised return to June 2029 at 12.25x to 13x becomes arithmetically available: EUR 63 to 67 of value against an entry price of EUR 44 to 46. That entry zone coincides with the March and June 2026 lows (EUR 47 to 48) and the 52-week low (EUR 42.55).

Where I differ from the market. Consensus targets imply +16% in twelve months, with the multiple held or raised. The model says the multiple is the risk and the earnings are the cushion. I agree with the model's structure, but I would make its earnings term slightly smaller (because of minorities) and its multiple term slightly less severe (13x rather than 12.25x). Those two changes give about -2% to -5% over 18 months: a stock that goes nowhere while the business doubles its EBIT from FY25.

What would change my view. Evidence for the 14x to 16x frame (a fourth-quarter cash beat, a reclassification signal or a Minsait partnership) would move the 18-month return to +6% to +23%. A price of EUR 44 to 48 would make the return attractive on the guideline multiple alone.

Conclusion: the model's -7.3% over 18 months and +5.5% over three years reflect earnings growth of 22% and 38% swamped by a 25% de-rating to the guideline multiple, and they are the right central reading at EUR 60; the return turns clearly positive only if the multiple holds, which needs a cash proof or a reclassification that the company is unlikely to deliver within 18 months, or at an entry price in the mid-40s.
Score: 19, set by the Rater. A loss gives F, and -7.3% maps to about 18-19. The Analyst's own 13x adjustment (-2% to -5%) and the 20% reinforcing scenario lift it slightly, while attributable EPS (-13%) and a fat lower tail (11x gives -17%, the severe case -40%) pull it down, so I hold it near the mapped point.

#13 Summary conclusion

Indra is a good business becoming a better one, inside a difficult share.

The profit engine is contracted, pre-financed and mechanical. A EUR 22bn backlog is converting at the limit of capacity, the mix is shifting toward an electronics business with a 20% margin, EBIT compounds at about 14% a year to 2030, and attributable EPS compounds at about 12%. FY26 will show a clean beat in February.

Three structural features cap what the shares can pay for that engine.

  1. Cash: the cash that funds the growth is customer money that Indra repays by offset from 2027, so reported cash conversion falls to about 0.6x while consensus assumes 0.9x.
  2. The state: the state that grants the moat also caps pricing, decides leadership and, through minority partners, takes a rising share of the growth.
  3. The multiple: at the 97th percentile of the stock's own history, the multiple already discounts a re-rating to a defence frame that Indra has not yet earned through cash conversion or index classification.

The order cycle has turned while the earnings cycle has two years to run, and in the defence sector share prices have historically followed the order cycle. The next four months (Capital Markets Day, election, fourth-quarter cash and FY27 guidance) decide whether the stock stays in Broadening or tips into Stalling; my weighting is 45% Stalling, 35% Broadening and 20% Reinforcing.

Reclassification is the one lever with the power to change the market's frame. Aerospace and defence pass half of revenue in FY27, so reclassification is plausible, but it is unscheduled; it is the reason to keep Indra on close watch rather than to own it at EUR 60.

The practical conclusion: the earnings are the cushion and the multiple is the risk; the setup Richard looks for appears at EUR 44 to 48, after a conservative FY27 guidance reset, or on a reclassification signal, and not before.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 76, set by the Rater. Strong, legislated and contracted external forces (80) and a large, funded internal pivot (68) are already turning into forecast profits (EPS about 12% a year, B at 80, EBIT margin rising well above any past level), so the net change is clearly positive and sure to reach profits for two to three years. It stays below Richard's Arteche 80 because order intake has peaked, the internal change enables rather than adds earnings and there is no beat-and-raise record under the new team, and EPS leaks to minorities and tax.
Foundations' Robustness: 58, set by the Rater. Quality at 58 rests on a protected industry and real sovereign and air-traffic moats but a state-granted home moat, no pricing power, low sustainment annuity, weak cash conversion and a new, state-led management, and the delivery record (62) is good historically but thin now, so the foundations are above typical yet not stable or predictable in Richard's CVS sense. Comparable with Judges Scientific's 60 (protected niches, budget-dependent demand), a touch lower for the poorer cash and governance.
Setups' Fit/Crispness: 66, set by the Rater. The case fits Demand-driven EPSU in substance: a legislated, funded demand step-up with a 3.4x backlog converting into revenue and margin; consensus and price holding the step-up do not count here. But two elements are loose today: capacity is still being built and delivery is already straining (TESS Dragon shortfall and penalty, 3Q Defence revenue 17% light), and half the revenue sits in a Minsait business the setup's mechanism does not describe, so it sits well below Richard's textbook Arteche 95 and below a one-loose-element 75.
Case Riskiness: 36, set by the Rater. Riskiness at 40 shows few drivers inside a complex chassis with correlated risks through one customer, one financing mechanism and one ramp and an EPS range of about -18%/+13%, and on top of that the share price carries a 97th-percentile multiple and a crowded defence theme, which Richard counts as the main risk of a large fall at Arteche 60. Indra adds a new, non-defence chief executive, a live leadership risk after the election, execution problems now and legal questions on the pre-financing, so it sits well below Arteche though above Judges Scientific's 20, whose end market is itself the problem.

The five judgements that move the shares most, with the arithmetic

The multiple is by far the largest swing: each turn is worth about EUR 4.5 a share. Among earnings judgements, Defence conversion is the largest and is asymmetric, and the below-the-line items together rival it.

Base: FY27 attributable EPS EUR 3.23 (model EUR 3.41 before minorities); 175.5m shares; tax rate 27%; Defence revenue EUR 3.0bn, of which TESS about EUR 0.85bn; two-year-forward EPS at December 2027 about EUR 4.49 (model).

1. Defence conversion pace in FY27: the largest operating swing, and an asymmetric one.

  • A 10% shortfall (EUR 300m), with plants and engineers already in place, drops through at 25% to 30%: EBIT falls by EUR 75m to 90m (group margin from 11.0% to about 9.9%), after-tax profit by EUR 55m to 66m, and EPS by EUR 0.31 to 0.37 (-10% to -11%).
  • A 10% beat drops through at about 18%: EBIT rises by EUR 54m and EPS by EUR 0.22 (+7%).
What to watchDefence revenue against about EUR 750m a quarter; Dragon acceptances; the phasing of Eurofighter and FCAS revenue (EUR 80m in 3Q26 against EUR 160m a quarter earlier).

2. The Defence margin, split the right way between TESS and the rest of Defence.

  • Defence excluding TESS (about EUR 2.15bn at about 20%): each 2 points of margin is EUR 43m of EBIT, EUR 31m after tax and EUR 0.18 of EPS (5.5%).
  • TESS (about EUR 0.85bn near zero): a margin stuck at 0% against a 2% base costs EUR 17m of EBIT but only EUR 6m of attributable profit after tax and the 49% minority, or EUR 0.04 of EPS (1.3%); a 5% margin adds EUR 0.05.
  • Upside case: if the margin excluding TESS holds near 20% through the ramp and TESS reaches 5% to 8% by FY29, the FY28-29 Defence margin is 17% rather than 16%, worth about EUR 40m of EBIT and EUR 0.13 of EPS. Serial-production precedents at Rheinmetall, Iveco Defence and General Dynamics show margins of 11% to 14%.

3. Below the line (tax, minorities and financial items) can move FY27 EPS by ±10% without a single operating variable changing, which is why the quality of the FY26 beat matters more than its size.

  • Tax: each point of tax rate is about EUR 0.045 of EPS (1.4%). A 25% rate instead of 27% adds EUR 0.09 (+2.8%); Bernstein's 2027 assumption of 30% takes away EUR 0.14 (-4%).
  • Minorities: EUR 15m (Bernstein) instead of EUR 28m adds EUR 0.07 (+2.3%); EUR 40m takes away EUR 0.07.
  • Net financial items: ±EUR 20m moves EPS by ±EUR 0.08.
  • The interest subsidy on zero-interest pre-financing (EUR 45m to 65m before tax, EUR 0.19 to 0.27 of EPS) fades over FY27-30.

4. The multiple: the largest swing of all. Each turn of multiple is worth about EUR 4.5 a share (7.5%) at December 2027. A fall from 16.3x to 12.25x is -25%, to 14x is -14%, and to 11x is -33%. A GICS reclassification (the revenue test is passed in FY27, with a review in 2028) or a Minsait partnership could hold or lift the multiple toward the 14x to 16x frame (+6% to +23% over 18 months). A fourth-quarter cash miss, a reset charge or a post-election leadership change could take the multiple to 11x (-17%). The March 2026 governance episode, when the shares fell nearly 30% in days while the sector moved differently, shows how fast an idiosyncratic multiple can move.

Each turn of multiple is about EUR 4.5 a share: the multiple dwarfs every earnings judgement above.

5. Cash and the advances: no effect on EPS, but a strong effect on the narrative and the multiple. On precedent (Rheinmetall, Saab), the cash narrative, not the earnings narrative, sets the multiple for a contractor in a ramp.

  • The fourth quarter: the FY26 floor needs more than EUR 305m of comparable free cash flow. Below EUR 250m is a miss that matters for the thesis; above EUR 350m rehabilitates the cash story for a quarter.
  • From FY27: the model's reported free cash flow of EUR 355m (0.6x net income) against consensus comparable free cash flow of EUR 514m is a 1.5-point difference in free cash flow yield (3.4% against 4.9% on a market value of EUR 10.6bn).
  • The quiet reason is capital spending above the guided ratio: EUR 374m in nine months, including the Paz II satellites financed by a EUR 1,011m repayable state loan. I have raised the model's capital-spending inputs for it (end note 6).

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
